main.summary: The Foolish Old Man of the North Mountain, nearly ninety, resolves to level the mountains Taihang and Wangwu that block his way. Ignoring the sneers of the Wise Old Man, he answers that his descendants will go on without end, and in the end Heaven is moved and has the two mountains carried away.
main.translation:
The two mountains Taihang and Wangwu were each seven hundred li square and ten thousand ren high. They stood originally south of Jizhou and north of Heyang. The Foolish Old Man of the North Mountain was nearly ninety, and lived facing the mountains. He was troubled that the mountains in the north blocked the way, so that going out and coming in meant a long detour. He gathered his household and made a plan: 'I and you will use all our strength to level the steep ground, make a way straight through to the south of Yu, and reach the south bank of the Han - what do you say?' They all agreed together.
His wife raised a doubt: 'With your strength you could not even reduce the hill of Kuifu; what could you do about Taihang and Wangwu? And where would you put the earth and stones?' They all said: 'Throw them into the tail of the Bohai Sea, to the north of Yintu.'
So he led his sons and grandsons, three men who could carry loads, and they broke the stones and dug the earth, and carried it in baskets and dust-pans to the tail of the Bohai Sea. A neighbour, the widow of a man of the Jingcheng family, had a small son who was just losing his milk teeth; he skipped off to help them. With the changing of cold and hot seasons, they made one trip there and back.
The Wise Old Man of Hequ laughed and tried to stop them, saying: 'How very foolish you are! With your remaining years and the little strength you have left, you cannot destroy so much as a hair of the mountain; what can you do with the earth and stones?' The Foolish Old Man of the North Mountain gave a long sigh and said: 'Your mind is truly set, so set that nothing can pierce it; you are not even as good as a widow and her small child. Even if I die, I have sons surviving; my sons will have grandsons, and the grandsons will have sons; their sons will have sons, and their sons will have grandsons; sons and grandsons will go on without end, while the mountain does not grow any higher. Why should I worry that it will not be levelled?' The Wise Old Man of Hequ had no answer.
The god who holds the snakes heard of it and, fearing that they would not stop, reported it to the Lord on High. The Lord was moved by his sincerity, and ordered the two sons of Kua'e to carry the two mountains on their backs, one to be set down east of Shuo, the other in the south of Yong. From then on, south of Ji and south of the Han, there were no hills left standing in the way.

keyLines.line: 北山愚公者，年且九十，面山而居
keyLines.en: The Foolish Old Man of the North Mountain was nearly ninety, and lived facing the mountains.
keyLines.note: It gives the person and his situation: a very old man facing the great mountains, which is where the story starts.

keyLines.line: 吾與汝畢力平險，指通豫南，達于漢陰，可乎
keyLines.en: I and you will use all our strength to level the steep ground, make a way straight through to the south of Yu, and reach the south bank of the Han - what do you say?
keyLines.note: The Foolish Old Man puts forward his plan to move the mountains, in order to open a road.

keyLines.line: 以殘年餘力，曾不能毀山之一毛，其如土石何
keyLines.en: With your remaining years and the little strength you have left, you cannot destroy so much as a hair of the mountain; what can you do with the earth and stones?
keyLines.note: The Wise Old Man mocks him from a practical standpoint, and serves as a foil to bring out the Foolish Old Man's firmness.

keyLines.line: 雖我之死，有子存焉；子又生孫，孫又生子
keyLines.en: Even if I die, I have sons surviving; my sons will have grandsons, and the grandsons will have sons.
keyLines.note: The Foolish Old Man answers with the idea of the generations handing the task on; this is the core of the argument.

keyLines.line: 子子孫孫無窮匱也，而山不加增，何苦而不平
keyLines.en: Sons and grandsons will go on without end, while the mountain does not grow any higher. Why should I worry that it will not be levelled?
keyLines.note: The moral: if one does not give up, even the hardest thing can be done in the end.

keyLines.line: 帝感其誠，命夸蛾氏二子負二山
keyLines.en: The Lord was moved by his sincerity, and ordered the two sons of Kua'e to carry the two mountains on their backs.
keyLines.note: The tale ends in myth, to show that sincerity can move heaven and earth.

glossary.note: An ancient unit of length; in the Zhou, eight chi made one ren.

glossary.en: He yang - north of the Yellow River
glossary.note: The area on the north bank of the Yellow River.
The name of a small hill.

glossary.en: Bo hai zhi wei, Yin tu zhi bei - the tail of the Bohai, north of Yintu
glossary.note: Legendary far-off places, used to mean somewhere very distant.
A winnowing basket and a dust-pan, tools for carrying earth.
Just starting to change the baby teeth, meaning a child of seven or eight.

glossary.en: He qu zhi sou - the Wise Old Man of Hequ
glossary.note: An old man living at a bend of the Yellow River, called Zhi Sou, 'wise old man', as a contrast to the 'foolish old man'.
A legendary god of great strength.

main.background: This piece comes from the Liezi, the chapter 'Questions of Tang'. It is a fable from the Daoist writings before the Qin (221 BC) in which the contrast between the Foolish Old Man and the Wise Old Man shows the spirit of perseverance. Later the phrase 'the Foolish Old Man moves the mountains' came to describe a will that fears no hardship and keeps on.
